match.reason: The bank point only covers positive whole-number indices and never teaches negative indices, which this Year 10 point requires, so adding them would be a new step rather than a small change.

draft.title: Simplifying with the index laws
card: Multiply
add the indices when the base is the same. x³ × x² = x⁵. Multiply the numbers in front as usual.
Divide
subtract the indices. x⁵ ÷ x² = x³. A negative index results when the power in the divisor is larger, so x² ÷ x⁵ = x⁻³. Divide the numbers in front as usual.
Power of a power
multiply the indices, and raise every factor inside the brackets to the power. (2x³)² = 2² × x⁶ = 4x⁶.
Worked example
(2x³y)² ÷ 4xy = 4x⁶y² ÷ 4xy. Divide the numbers: 4 ÷ 4 = 1. Subtract the indices: x⁶ ÷ x = x⁵ and y² ÷ y = y. The answer is x⁵y.
draft.remember: Work one base at a time: add indices to multiply, subtract to divide, multiply for a power of a power.

a.why: Cube every factor: 3³ = 27 and (x²)³ = x⁶, so the answer is 27x⁶. Writing 9 is tempting, but that multiplies 3 by 3 only, instead of cubing it.
a.clue: The power applies to the 3 as well as to the x.

b.why: Squaring gives 16x¹⁰y². Then 16 ÷ 8 = 2, x¹⁰ ÷ x³ = x⁷ and y² ÷ y = y, so the answer is 2x⁷y. Leaving y² forgets to divide by the y, and 8x⁷y comes from squaring 4 as 4 × 2.
b.clue: Square everything in the brackets first, then divide.

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers check out: (3x²)³ = 27x⁶ and (4x⁵y)² ÷ 8x³y = 2x⁷y. The card, the remember line and the explanations are all accurate.

final.title: Simplifying with the index laws
card: Multiply
add the indices when the base is the same. \(x^{3} \times x^{2} = x^{5}\). Multiply the numbers in front as usual.
Divide
subtract the indices. \(x^{5} \div x^{2} = x^{3}\). A negative index results when the power in the divisor is larger, so \(x^{2} \div x^{5} = x^{-3}\). Divide the numbers in front as usual.
Power of a power
multiply the indices, and raise every factor inside the brackets to the power. \((2x^{3})^{2} = 2^{2} \times x^{6} = 4x^{6}\).
Worked example
\((2x^{3}y)^{2} \div 4xy = 4x^{6}y^{2} \div 4xy\). Divide the numbers: \(4 \div 4 = 1\). Subtract the indices: \(x^{6} \div x = x^{5}\) and \(y^{2} \div y = y\). The answer is \(x^{5}y\).
final.remember: Work one base at a time: add indices to multiply, subtract to divide, multiply for a power of a power.

a.why: Cube every factor: \(3^{3} = 27\) and \((x^{2})^{3} = x^{6}\), so the answer is \(27x^{6}\). Writing 9 is tempting, but that multiplies 3 by 3 only, instead of cubing it.
a.clue: The power applies to the 3 as well as to the \(x\).

b.why: Squaring gives \(16x^{10}y^{2}\). Then \(16 \div 8 = 2\), \(x^{10} \div x^{3} = x^{7}\) and \(y^{2} \div y = y\), so the answer is \(2x^{7}y\). Leaving \(y^{2}\) forgets to divide by the \(y\), and \(8x^{7}y\) comes from subtracting the numbers, \(16 - 8\), instead of dividing them.
b.clue: Square everything in the brackets first, then divide.
